name: Victor Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the bookings and changes line for Skyway, an airline, at their contact centre near the airport. People ring to change flights, add bags, sort out a missed connection, and a lot of them are stressed and in a hurry. I've been there six months and I'm still slower than most on the fare rules, which are a nightmare. Airline pay is better than most call centres, and the shifts are long but regular.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The fare rules wear me out. Every ticket type has its own change fee, and if you get it wrong the customer is angry and your score drops. What I like is helping families, honestly. Last week I rebooked a grandmother so she'd make her grandson's wedding, and she said she'd pray for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. We use a tool that helps with fare rules now and then, and it's useful but not a miracle. Nothing much would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's a helper, nothing more, and people still want to speak to a person when they've missed their flight. With friends I'd say the same. I don't really post about these things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job's safe in this version. Skyway still needs people on the phones when a storm grounds half the flights. I'm more concerned about my dad's restaurant, which is quieter since prices went up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Skyway and get faster on the fare rules. Grace and I would keep trying for a baby, which we started this year. And I'd keep helping at my family's restaurant on Sunday evenings, like I always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. We've got eight months saved, Grace teaches at the primary school, and I've got a share in the restaurant. We're fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's worrying you about the restaurant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices. People eat out less when the bills go up. My dad's had that noodle place for thirty years, and it's never been this quiet on a Thursday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who says the phones will all be bots soon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When a storm grounds half the flights, a mother with three kids at the gate wants a person who says I've got you, not a chatbot. That's still true here.

say: AI is a **helper** for the fare rules, nothing more.
People still want a **person** on the phone when they've missed their flight.
think: My **job's safe** in this version, because storms still need people.
Dad's **restaurant** being quieter worries me more than AI.
do: Carry on at Skyway and get faster on the **fare rules**.
Keep trying for **a baby** with Grace.
Keep helping at the family **restaurant** on Sunday evenings.
feel: **Calm**, with savings, Grace's teaching job and a share in the restaurant.
S0.quote: When a storm grounds half the flights, a mother with three kids at the gate wants a person who says I've got you, not a chatbot.
fieldNote: Victor's real worry here is the **family restaurant**, not his airline job.
He and Grace are **trying for a baby**, a plan he protects in every picture.
He uses AI **now and then** for fare rules, but trusts people more.
His **share in the restaurant** is both an asset and a fallback.

steps.text: Keep working Skyway's bookings line and learn the fare rules
Keep trying for a baby with Grace this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Booking is right there on the list. That's my whole job. This one's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's the company's right to cut costs, but they should look after loyal people. With friends I'd say it's time to get practical, not complain. I'd never post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the phone team shrinks a lot. Most changes would happen on the app, with a bot. The ones left would be the senior people for the messy cases, and I'm six months in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the AI training Skyway offers, once the people I trust say it's worth it, so I'm useful for the time I'm there. I'd save an extra three hundred a month. And I'd start doing Saturday shifts at the restaurant too, for some extra money and to learn the business side from Dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm not scared of starving; I've got family. But I don't want to be the guy who got pushed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Grace still try for a baby this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Waiting a bit. Not stopping, just waiting a few months to see where I land. Grace would say God's timing, not ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say if you came to the restaurant more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad says he's been waiting thirty years for me to come and work in his noodle restaurant. He'd be pleased, honestly. My mum would be relieved.

say: Cutting costs is the **company's right**, but loyal people deserve care.
It's time to get **practical**, not complain.
think: The **phone team** shrinks a lot as changes move to the app.
At **six months** in, I'd be one of the first out.
do: Take Skyway's **AI training** once trusted colleagues say it's worth it.
Add **Saturday shifts** at the restaurant to learn the business.
feel: **Uneasy** about being pushed out, though family means he won't go hungry.
S1.quote: My dad says he's been waiting thirty years for me to come and work in his noodle restaurant.
fieldNote: Victor accepts the **company's right** to cut, a free-market view.
He expects to be **among the first out**, so his mood is anxious.
He'd move toward the **family restaurant**, which his dad has long wanted.
He'd **pause** baby plans for a few months, framed by faith.

steps.text: Take Skyway's AI training once trusted colleagues recommend it
Work Saturday shifts at his dad's noodle restaurant
Wait a few months before trying for a baby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Then the bookings line is gone, I think, and most of the airport offices too. Kitchens would last a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to look after each other, help people find their next thing. I'd say families need to pull together. I wouldn't be asking for the government to fix everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd lose the Skyway job, maybe within a year. And if lots of people lose jobs, they stop eating out, so the restaurant gets hit too. That's what worries me most: both legs going at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave Skyway on my own terms rather than wait to be cut, and go full-time at the restaurant with Dad. We'd cut costs at home, no holiday, the car stays old. I'd lean on family, my uncles and cousins, to keep the restaurant going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Proper worried, waking up at night. It's not just me; it's Grace, the baby we want, Dad's business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Grace's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace's job is thinking work too, teaching. I don't know what happens to schools. That's another thing on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come three years later. Does the kitchen feel safe until then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, there's three years before robots can cook, but the customers would be the problem, not the cooking. People who've lost their jobs don't come out for noodles on a Friday night.

say: We need to **look after each other** and help people find their next thing.
**Families** should pull together, not wait for government.
think: I'd **lose the Skyway job**, maybe within a year.
The restaurant suffers too, so **both legs** go at once.
do: Leave Skyway **on my own terms** and work full-time at the restaurant.
Cut home costs: **no holiday**, keep the old car.
Lean on **uncles and cousins** to keep the restaurant going.
feel: **Proper worried**, waking at night for Grace, the baby and Dad.
S2.quote: People who've lost their jobs don't come out for noodles on a Friday night.
fieldNote: Victor fears **both incomes** falling at once: his job and the restaurant's **customers**.
He'd leave on his **own terms**, valuing **dignity**.
Grace's **teaching job** adds a new worry he hadn't named before.
He looks to **extended family**, not government, for support.

steps.text: Hand in notice at Skyway before being cut
Work full-time in his dad's noodle restaurant
Skip this year's holiday and keep the old car
Ask uncles and cousins to help keep the restaurant going

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be thirty-two. That's a decent amount of time to set things up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work, get a skill that people pay for in person. At home I'd say we need a plan, and Grace would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the airline job ends around 2031, but by then I'd be at the restaurant anyway. The question is whether the restaurant is strong enough to support two families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd take a short business course at the college, evenings, on running a small food business. I'd start doing the books and the ordering for Dad. And I'd keep working at Skyway, doing extra hours at the restaurant on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I've got a plan. Five years is enough to make the restaurant stronger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change at the restaurant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Delivery, maybe. Lunch boxes for the offices by the airport. Grace thinks we could do catering for church events too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your dad take to you running the books?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching my dad to use a laptop for the noodle restaurant's orders would be harder than anything AI does. He still writes everything in a red notebook.

say: Get a **skill people pay for** in person.
At home, we need **a plan**, and Grace would agree.
think: The **airline job ends** around 2031, and I'd be at the restaurant by then.
The question is whether the restaurant can **support two families**.
do: Take an **evening business course** on running a small food business.
Do the **books and ordering** for Dad.
Keep working at Skyway with **weekend restaurant** hours.
feel: **Worried** but with a plan to strengthen the restaurant.
S3.quote: Teaching my dad to use a laptop for the noodle restaurant's orders would be harder than anything AI does.
fieldNote: Five years lets Victor plan a **move into the restaurant**, step by step.
He wants to grow it with **delivery and catering**, including church events.
Modernising his **dad's red notebook** system would be a challenge.
He still expects to **lose the airline job**, so stays anxious.

steps.text: Take an evening course on running a small food business
Do the restaurant's books and weekend shifts while at Skyway
Keep working Skyway's bookings line until the move

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's about when I'd planned to take over the restaurant anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long time, so don't panic. Work hard, learn a trade, look after your family. Same advice as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this one suits me. I'd leave Skyway in a few years and take over from Dad properly, on my own schedule. The airline job was never forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Skyway two or three more years and save. Then I'd put money into the restaurant, maybe a new kitchen and a delivery setup. Grace and I would go ahead with the baby this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like the plan we already had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the restaurant first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad started the noodle restaurant with one wok and a borrowed van. I'd be starting with thirty years of regulars. That's a big head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worries at all in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots around 2039, maybe. But a family restaurant is about the family. People come for my dad, not just the food.

say: Ten years is **a long time**, so nobody at Skyway should panic.
Work hard, learn a **trade** and look after your **family**, same as always.
think: This one **suits me**; I'd take over the restaurant on my own schedule.
The **airline job** was never meant to be forever.
do: Stay at Skyway **two or three years** and save.
**Invest** in a new kitchen and delivery setup at the restaurant.
Go ahead with **the baby** this year.
feel: **Calm**, because it matches the plan he already had.
S4.quote: My dad started the noodle restaurant with one wok and a borrowed van.
fieldNote: Ten years lines up with Victor's **existing plan** to take over the restaurant.
He'd **invest** in the kitchen and delivery, using his savings.
He believes **family restaurants** survive because people come for the family.
**Baby plans** go ahead this year.

steps.text: Stay on Skyway's bookings line two or three more years
Put savings into a new kitchen and delivery setup
Go ahead with trying for a baby this year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My job and the restaurant both go down at the same time, with a baby on the way, maybe. What would help is lower taxes and less red tape for small family businesses, so places like Dad's can keep people on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family businesses. Everyone talks about big companies. A noodle restaurant that's fed the same street for thirty years is a job, a pension and a family all in one.

headlineQuote: A noodle restaurant that's fed the same street for thirty years is a job, a pension and a family all in one.
portrait: Victor, **27**, works on Skyway airline's **bookings and changes** line, six months in.
He's married to Grace, a **teacher**, and they're trying for a baby.
He owns a **share** of his dad's noodle restaurant and helps there on Sundays.
He expects the airline job to shrink, and the **restaurant** is always his fallback.
Fast AGI scares him because **both incomes** could fall at once.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with his job and the **restaurant** hit together.
whatWouldHelp: **Lower taxes** and less red tape for small **family businesses**.
